ety.text: From Middle English gasen; akin to Swedish dialectal gasa and Gothic 𐌿𐍃𐌲𐌰𐌹𐍃𐌾𐌰𐌽 (usgaisjan, “to terrify”).

ex: They gazed at the stars for hours.
Why stand ye gazing up into heaven?
Strait toward Heav'n my wondring Eyes I turnd, / And gaz'd a while the ample Skie

I searched for form and land
For years and years I roamed
I gazed a gazeless stare.

senses.d: A fixed look; a look of eagerness, wonder, or admiration; a continued look of attention.

ex: Those howers that with gentle worke did frame / The louely gaze where euery eye doth dwell.
Made of my Enemies the ſcorn and gaze;

senses.d: In Lacanian psychoanalysis, the relationship of the subject with the desire to look and awareness that one can be viewed.
ex: She counters the tendency to focus on critical strategies of resisting the male gaze, raising the issue of the female spectator.

senses.d: The framework in which a subject is presented, determined by the biases of the creator and/or audience.
ex: The American panorama is indicative of the nation's expansion westward and an example of the American gaze.
A Poulsbo woman who found herself surrounded by a gaze of raccoons Monday has regained her home.

ety.text: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin wardāre.
Inherited from Middle French regard, from Old French regard, from reguarder.
From Vulgar Latin *oculāta, ultimately from Latin oculus (“eye”). Or by surface analysis, occhio + -ata.
From Old Galician-Portuguese aollar, from Vulgar Latin *adoculāre, from oclus, from Latin oculus. Cognate with Galician ollar, Mirandese oulhar, Spanish aojar and Italian adocchiare.

Borrowed from French gazette, from Italian gazzetta, from Venetan gazeta, from gazeta dele novità (literally “a gazeta (halfpenny) of news”), named for the cost (one gazeta) of the newspaper. Compare penny dreadful, dime novel. See gazzetta for more.

senses.d: A newspaper; a printed sheet published periodically.
An official periodical publication published by a government containing legal and state notices, and in some cases, legislations, subsidiary legislations and bills.
To announce the status of (someone) in an official gazette; this pertained to both appointments and bankruptcies.
ex: Benjamin had already been gazetted captain and Kopp was in process of being gazetted major.

ety.text: Borrowed in the 17th century from Venetan gazeta (“newspaper”), from gazeta dele novità (literally “a gazeta (halfpenny) of news”), named for the cost (one gazeta) of the newspaper. The etymology of the coin’s name is disputed.

phr: have one's name in the Gazette
